title: Americans Suddenly Fell in Love with Japan — Not Because It's Cheap, Because It's Normal
dek: The real driver of Japan's tourism explosion isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space — clean subways, on time, no trash. What American visitors experience in Tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused.
why: This episode uses expert interviews plus a listener survey to break "why is everyone going to Japan" into six verifiable reasons; the back half, on Japanese craft culture versus American dysfunction, is especially worth hearing.
who: People curious about the Japan tourism phenomenon, founders and investors making calls on consumer and cultural trends, and readers who want to understand the contrast with American social dysfunction.

points.body: The questioner, Lisa, is a Japanese person living in Tokyo. She made a visitor calendar from November 2022 to April 2026, with green cells marking when someone came to visit. She counted 119 people, 96 of them her own guests, averaging one person every five days, 20% of all her days. She says she spends all her free time helping visiting friends plan itineraries. This data visualization is itself evidence that the problem has spun out of control, and it's the starting point for the question this episode sets out to answer.

points.h: Japan is poor in resources, rich in story
points.body: Roland Kelts argues the first reason for American interest in Japan isn't economic, it's story. He says Japan has almost no natural resources, no oil, very little land, only small rice paddies, but a story culture that is astonishing. The world's first novel is Japanese, The Tale of Genji, a thousand years old. Through manga, anime and the internet, the whole world discovered this narrative capacity. This didn't start in the 1990s; Roland says there were two earlier waves: Japanism in late 19th-century Europe, and the Beats' and hippies' fascination with Zen and Buddhist concepts in the 50s and 60s.

David Marks points out that for seventy years after World War II, mainstream American feeling toward Japan was fear, not affection. Before 1945 Japan was an enemy nation; afterward it was seen as a developing country rebuilding itself. In the 70s and 80s it became anxiety about Japanese economic power, and Michael Crichton's Rising Sun cast Japan as the villain. After the Cold War ended there was even a CIA position paper discussing whether Japan should become the next enemy. When Japan's economic bubble burst in the 90s, America actually felt a sense of relief. When David moved to Japan in 2003, having a friend visit Japan was the event of the year, because nobody came at all.

points.h: The government made Japan cheap by hand
points.body: The third wave was a government plan. In 2003 Junichiro Koizumi launched the Visit Japan campaign, with a target raised from 5 million tourists a year to 10 million, and ads full of Western stereotypes: geisha, cherry blossoms, temples. But what really worked was Shinzo Abe deliberately weakening the yen in the 2010s. The intent was to help exports; the result was making hotels and restaurants cheap for foreigners. Roland says in Tokyo you can eat a very good soba lunch for under $10, while in New York $10 won't even buy you an apple and a banana. In 2013 Abe relaxed visas for Thailand and Malaysia, then China and Indonesia; Asian tourists surged first, and European and American tourists followed.

points.h: Japan's functionality is the biggest draw
points.body: Roland says the most important reason is functionality. Public space in many countries, especially the United States, has become disabled: parks are dirty and dangerous, rail systems are terrible, airports are a mess. In Japan, things just work. PJ adds that American ears hear complaints about poor public order and dirty subways as elitism, as rich people's complaints. But in Japan, wanting the subway to be clean isn't elitism — it's the reverse: why shouldn't public things be good? On Tokyo streets you see no trash, not even cigarette butts, and you don't smell urine or feces. PJ says this isn't the reason for a first trip, but it may be the reason some people go again.

points.h: Japan worships the people who make things, not the people who sell them
points.body: The sixth reason is craft. The Japanese word shokunin means artisan, someone who can make things extremely well, and such people are still respected in Japan, a status traceable to the 17th-century Edo period, when makers outranked merchants. Roland tells of an animation industry person explaining the Walmart model to him: in America, the company selling the goods comes first, nobody cares who made it, and a $5 pillow was made by someone who knows nothing about pillows. But in Japan, the person who makes a pillow extremely well is the most valuable. He took an American friend to a ramen shop, where you queue to buy a ticket, and the ticket said come back at 3 p.m. After eating, the friend said it was the best soup of his life, then asked why they don't franchise. Roland said because franchising means you can't control the quality of the noodles, the scallions, the pork bone broth and the bamboo shoots — their scallions come from a man named Sato in Chiba who has done this for many years.

points.h: The listener survey and the experts almost perfectly overlap
points.body: Search Engine sent a questionnaire to hundreds of thousands of listeners and got a huge number of replies. Nearly half mentioned culture; some said they binge-watched anime growing up, played Nintendo and Sony, and are fans of Pokemon and One Piece. About a quarter mentioned the weak yen; one said the exchange rate is the best in 30 years. Others mentioned craft. What made PJ happiest were the reasons only a big survey could capture: someone decided to go because of FOMO after seeing so many people go, someone went to see the Godzilla museum, and Godzilla brought in five listeners. There were also one-to-one stories: someone went to Japan to see the work of the legendary bonsai master Mazuhiko Kimura; someone fell in love with a person at 18, lost touch more than a decade later, and the only way to see them again was to fly to Japan, and ended up spending four magical days in Osaka.

points.h: Japan is a place where entropy has been paused
points.body: Listener enthusiasm for functionality exceeded PJ's expectations. One said they took their family to Japan to show them what a high-functioning society actually looks like, everything on time, perfectly clean. One said public toilets are everywhere and have bidet functions, because everyone has to poop, and a poop butt is disgusting. One said the world would be much better if every country respected each other the way Japanese people do with their punctuality and queuing. PJ himself says he still loves America, loves that anarchic mixture, but feels something broke about ten years ago — not just politics; drivers are angrier, people are angrier, elbows are sharper, and more people watch TikTok on the subway without headphones. He says America is like an eccentric friend who turned from quirky to not-so-good quirky, and that makes Japan's appeal understandable.

quotes.text: My question was, why is every single person I know going to Japan or talking about going to Japan?

I often say that Japan is very poor in natural resources. There's no oil here, very little land. You know, you can grow rice, but only in these tiny rice paddies. It's a small country, but it's very rich in stories.

A lot of countries around the world, particularly the U.S., have become dysfunctional. And I say that in terms of public space. The parks are dirty and dangerous. The railway system is atrocious. The airports are a mess. And when you're in Japan, things just work.
In America, one way you can show you care about society is to ride the dirty subway. In Japan, one way you can show you care about society is to be really invested in the subway being clean.

He said, so if you go into Walmart, you can buy a $5 pillow. And it was made by people who know nothing about pillows. They don't care about pillows. They're working in some factory in Southeast Asia or China. And he said, that's the Walmart model. But he said, in Japan, we actually think the person who made the pillow and made it really well is the most valuable person.
I took my family to Japan so they could see what a high-functioning society really looks like, where everything runs on time, is perfectly clean.
